cards.headline: Developments in the Gaza Strip one year after ceasefire implementation

pages.text: One year after a ceasefire deal came into effect in the Gaza Strip, the territory lacks the promised international peacekeeping force and reconstruction efforts, according to reporting by NPR World. The deal followed efforts by President Donald Trump to push Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. While bombings have slowed during the ceasefire, Israel has continued targeting Hamas, and Gaza's Health Ministry reports that these attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians over the past year, including nearly 500 women and children. NPR reporter Anas Baba has documented moments of respite and grief throughout the 12-month period, including a Palestinian mother mourning her son at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City following an Israeli airstrike that occurred just over a month into the ceasefire.

The Israeli military has expanded its control to approximately 70% of Gaza, a development that has squeezed more than 2 million Palestinians toward the edge of the sea. Despite these conditions, increased food entry has helped reverse starvation across the territory, allowing residents to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of Gaza last year.

cards.headline: Mainstreet Research poll shows narrowing lead for Olivia Chow in Toronto mayoral race

pages.text: A Mainstreet Research poll released Friday suggests the mayoral race in Toronto is tightening between incumbent Olivia Chow and Councillor Brad Bradford. The survey, conducted on Oct. 6 and 7, placed Chow at 40.8 per cent support and Bradford at 38.3 per cent, following the withdrawal of Chris Alexander from the election. Quito Maggi, president and CEO of Mainstreet Research, told CBC News the results were “statistically tied” because the 2.5-point gap between the candidates is approximately the same as the survey's margin of error. Maggi noted that the Bradford campaign appears to have momentum and stated that the chances of a Chow re-election are becoming less certain with a short runway remaining. The poll also found that the difference between the two candidates narrowed to 2.9 points among decided and leaning voters, while 10 per cent of respondents remained undecided.

The results represent a shift from a Mainstreet Research poll at the end of September, which had placed Chow with a six-point lead over Bradford. In a news release, the Bradford campaign stated that Chow would allegedly rely on “scare tactics” until election day due to the narrowed divide in support. cards.headline: French archaeologist documents historic civilizations in AlUla, Saudi Arabia

pages.text: Laila Nehmé, a French archaeologist and research fellow with the French National Centre for Scientific Research, has been documenting the historic civilizations of AlUla, Saudi Arabia, since 2002. Working in cooperation with the Saudi Ministry of Culture, Nehmé specializes in the Nabataeans, an ancient Arab people, and the science of ancient writings known as epigraphy. Her research includes the study of Nabataean Aramaic, the language and script used by the Nabataeans for inscriptions on stone and papyri. Prior to her work in AlUla, Nehmé worked in Syria and at the ancient city of Petra in Jordan during the late 1980s and 1990s. According to Nehmé, the AlUla region contains heritage dating from the Paleolithic period approximately 200,000 years ago through to the 1980s, featuring sandstone cliff inscriptions in various scripts and rock art depicting human figures, cattle, and camels.

Nehmé reported to Arab News that excavations at the Hegra site, also known as Madain Salih or Al-Hijir, have yielded dozens of skeletons from several monumental tombs. She noted that some remains were remarkably well preserved due to the extremely dry climate and low humidity, with some skulls retaining hair, traces of skin along the spine, and fragments of leather or textile shrouds.

cards.headline: Police in Khulna, Bangladesh, instructed not to travel alone at night

pages.text: Police in the Khulna district of Bangladesh have been instructed not to travel alone at night following a knife attack that seriously injured a police inspector in Khulna city. The directive was issued in an official letter signed by the superintendent of police of the District Special Branch (DSB) on the night of October 9, 2026. The letter noted that special operations are underway in the Rupsa, Terokhada, Dighalia, and Batiaghata police station areas in response to the current law and order situation and several recent incidents, including attacks by criminals on law enforcement personnel. Unit in-charges were directed to take necessary measures to ensure the personal safety of personnel engaged in special operations and other duties. Copies of the directive were sent to all relevant offices and police stations under the district police. Khulna Superintendent of Police Sarker Omar Faruk told Prothom Alo that the restriction was imposed to prevent police personnel from falling victim to muggers while returning home after duty. When asked if the directive suggested police insecurity, Faruk stated the internal letter's main purpose is to ensure no personnel fall victim to muggers. The instruction follows an incident on October 9, 2026, at approximately 2:30 a.m., when 43-year-old Police Inspector Shah Alam was attacked by muggers in front of Khulna Collegiate School on Khan Jahan Ali Road. According to police sources, Alam was traveling by rickshaw in plain clothes after conducting a special operation in Rupsa upazila when three muggers intercepted him and attempted to snatch his money and mobile phones. When he resisted, the attackers struck both his wrists with a sharp machete. Alam was rescued by police and taken to a hospital, but as his condition deteriorated, he was transferred to a private hospital in Dhaka, where he remains under treatment in critical condition.

cards.headline: Trump asks US Supreme Court to revive dismissed lawsuit against Hillary Clinton

pages.text: On October 9, 2026, President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court to revive a dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival, Hillary Clinton. According to Arab News, Trump is accusing Clinton, former FBI Director James Comey, and others of conspiring to rig the 2016 election by linking his campaign to Russia. In the complaint, Trump alleged that Clinton and her allies used a “false narrative” regarding collusion with Russia to discredit his campaign. The legal action names several other defendants, including former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele and the Democratic National Committee.

The appeal follows a dismissal by US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks, who cited numerous inadequacies in the suit, including that Trump waited too long to bring certain claims. Judge Middlebrooks also imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers, characterizing the suit as “frivolous.” A US appeals court subsequently upheld both the dismissal and the sanctions. pages.text: The UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce (UKGCC), in partnership with the UK-Ghana Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET) Programme, has launched the UK-Ghana Trade Resource Centre. The platform aims to support firms in taking advantage of the UK-Ghana Trade Partnership Agreement (TPA) by providing guidance, market intelligence, and trade facilitation services.

The Trade Resource Centre will provide specific services for different business types. For export-ready Ghanaian businesses, the Centre is intended to offer market-specific guidance, export readiness support, referrals to technical expertise, and connections to British buyers and commercial networks. It will also work with partners to identify firms and facilitate business matchmaking. For importers and UK businesses looking to source from Ghana, the Centre will provide access to industry networks, partner referrals, and commercial linkage support to improve trade flows. cards.headline: Ashaiman Municipal Assembly lobbies for completion of storm-drain project in Ghana

pages.text: The Ashaiman Municipal Assembly in Ghana is appealing to authorities, including the Hydrological Services Agency, to complete a storm-drain project at the Gbemi Stream to mitigate flood risks. Freeman Tsekpo, the Municipal Chief Executive (MCE), stated that funding is the primary obstacle to finishing the construction. According to the Assembly, only approximately 150 metres of the planned storm drain approaching the Starlight Bridge has been completed since work began following the construction of the bridge in 2020, leaving a critical section of the watercourse unconstructed. The Assembly noted that periodic desilting of the existing drain does not provide a permanent solution to the municipality's flooding challenges. Ashaiman has experienced major flooding in 2010, with further incidents reported in 2018 and 2024. Mr. Tsekpo noted that extensive dredging and desilting at the Ajei Kojo underbridge helped prevent major flooding during heavy rains in 2025 and 2026, but emphasized that such measures cannot replace a properly engineered storm-drain system.

The Gbemi Stream also faces challenges from indiscriminate dumping. During a recent Municipal Assembly clean-up exercise, workers and machines were deployed to remove refuse from the watercourse. Mr. Tsekpo reported that residents living along the drain have used parts of it as a refuse dump, which reduces the capacity of the watercourse and increases the risk of obstruction during heavy rainfall. The Assembly is currently using additional workers and machinery to remove the refuse from the site.

cards.headline: Iraq rejects Syria's request to repatriate 4,000 suspected ISIS detainees

pages.text: Iraq has rejected a request from Syria to repatriate approximately 4,000 Syrian detainees suspected of links to the Islamic State (ISIS), according to Iraqi National Security Advisor Qasim al-Aboudi. The detainees were transferred from Syrian detention facilities to Iraqi custody earlier this year. Al-Aboudi told The Associated Press that Damascus requested the Syrian nationals be handed over for trial in Syria, but Baghdad declined the request. A recent meeting involving Iraqi, Syrian, and U.S. officials addressed the fate of the detainees. Al-Aboudi stated that hundreds of the Syrians currently held in Iraq are believed to be senior members of ISIS. He noted that Iraq is conducting investigations and that anyone proven to have committed crimes in Iraq will be tried under Iraqi law. Al-Aboudi added that detainees from countries that do not impose the death penalty would not face capital punishment in Iraq, and those convicted could potentially be transferred to their home countries to serve remaining sentences if prisoner-transfer agreements are in place.

Regarding the status of other detainees, al-Aboudi said Iraq has already returned approximately 50 Syrian detainees after determining they were not members of ISIS. Iraqi authorities have also identified about 400 Syrian detainees who were not affiliated with the group and could be released. Additionally, al-Aboudi stated that Baghdad has requested $500 million from the United States and other members of the international coalition against ISIS to assist with detention and prison-security costs. While the coalition has expressed willingness to provide support, Iraq has not yet received the funding. This detainee issue follows the end of the United States' 12-year military mission against ISIS in Iraq, with the final U.S. troops withdrawing from the country at the end of September.

cards.headline: Communities oppose waste-to-energy plant near Dhaka, Bangladesh

pages.text: Construction of a $467 million power plant designed to incinerate municipal waste for electricity near Dhaka, Bangladesh, is facing opposition from nearby communities over potential health risks from toxic air pollution, according to a report by Eyamin Sajid for Mongabay. The project, which is being overseen by the Dhaka North City Corporation and owned by the China Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC), is slated for completion in December 2028. The facility is intended to incinerate up to 3,000 metric tons of waste daily to generate up to 42.5 megawatts of electricity. Densely populated communities and several schools are located less than a mile from the site. Local farmers, including rice and vegetable grower Md Naim, told Mongabay that unmanaged trash fires at the current dumpsite already cause headaches and breathing difficulties due to smoke and ash.

An environmental impact assessment for the project states the incinerator will produce 74.8 metric tons of airborne fly ash daily. Additionally, an analysis by environmental groups indicates the plant will generate 39.56 metric tons of toxic substances annually, including heavy metals, dioxins, and furans, alongside 73,576 metric tons of solid waste. Hasan Mehedi, secretary of the Bangladesh Working Group on Ecology and Development (BWGED), stated that regular operation of the plant could lead to respiratory and lung-related problems, eye irritation, fatigue, and long-term health issues for local residents, particularly children and the elderly, due to chronic exposure to air pollution.

cards.headline: Ghana health ministry declares yellow fever outbreak in Upper West Region

pages.text: The Ministry of Health has declared a yellow fever outbreak in parts of the Upper West Region of Ghana following the laboratory confirmation of three cases, all of which resulted in deaths. Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh announced the declaration in Accra, stating that the confirmed cases were identified out of 450 suspected cases. The Ministry of Health is working through the Ghana Health Service and in partnership with the WHO to coordinate the response. The Ghana Health Service is scheduled to begin a mass vaccination campaign in the affected region next week, targeting individuals aged nine months to 60 years in the Sissala East, Sissala West, and Wa West districts. In response to the outbreak, the Ministry has activated National and Regional Public Health Emergency Operations Centres and deployed Rapid Response Teams for surveillance and case finding. Other implemented measures include promoting the use of insecticide-treated bed nets and repellents, strengthening case management at designated facilities, and intensifying community engagement. The Minister advised the public that yellow fever is not transmitted through direct person-to-person contact and urged citizens to report to health facilities if they experience sudden fever, headache, muscle pain, yellowing of the eyes or skin, or unusual bleeding.

cards.headline: Researchers say Britons are not being fully informed about climate and nature crisis

pages.text: Researchers say the British government must be honest about the scale of threats posed by climate and nature breakdown, following a study of viewers of the People’s Emergency Briefing. According to the research, 93% of 13,000 people surveyed said the public is not being fully informed about the climate crisis and nature loss. Professor Lorraine Whitmarsh of the University of Bath, who led the research, stated that while most people are aware of some climate risks, the “second-order risks” regarding food supplies, national security, and impacts on the NHS are not as obvious. The briefing, which was held last November at Central Hall in Westminster, featured nine experts providing assessments on the changes required for the UK to adapt to a changing climate and ecological landscape. The event was described as a “first-of-its-kind national emergency briefing.”

The People’s Emergency Briefing was a crowdfunded film outlining threats to public health, the economy, and food security. It has been viewed by an estimated 185,000 people across more than 3,400 screenings. Of those surveyed, 87% said watching the film increased their motivation to act, and the film is associated with a “substantial shift” in environmental concern and understanding. cards.headline: Study finds scientists with high faith in technology less likely to take climate action

pages.text: A study from the London School of Economics, published in Environmental Research Letters, found that scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action or lifestyle changes. The research surveyed more than 9,000 scientists across 115 countries regarding their views on “techno-optimism.” Of those surveyed, 27% agreed that technology will largely solve climate change problems, while 44% disagreed and 29% neither agreed nor disagreed. The report found that techno-optimism was most prevalent among scientists working in applied and natural sciences and those with right-leaning political views. Lead author Fabian Dablander stated that the belief in technological solutions can lead to an over-reliance on unproven solutions at the expense of necessary socioeconomic transformations, noting that technological solutions are often politically attractive because they do not require changes to how people live and consume.

According to the London School of Economics report, “techno-optimist” scientists are 23% less likely to sign petitions or participate in protests than peers who doubt technology is the answer. These scientists also reported engaging in less advocacy and fewer civic actions. Additionally, the study found that techno-optimists are 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, such as reducing flights, cutting car usage, or adopting a mostly vegan or vegetarian diet. Dablander noted that while technology cannot substitute for broader societal changes and large-scale shifts in consumption, there is a tendency at the individual level for greater faith in technological solutions to go hand in hand with less engagement in climate action.

cards.headline: Study finds land use changes after colonisation created a wildfire loop in south-east Australia

pages.text: Researchers have identified a “catastrophic wildfire loop” in south-east Australia, where land use changes following colonisation have increased susceptibility to climate-fuelled bushfires. According to a study published in Nature, the shift from open woodland to dense forest after 1788 led to more intense fires, a change consistent with the removal of the Gunaikurnai people from the land and the subsequent loss of cultural burning practices. Michael-Shawn Fletcher, a professor at the University of Melbourne and the study’s lead author, stated that land use changes occurred more than a century before climate changes, allowing shrubs to increase and fires to become hotter. These intense fires then trigger eucalypt recruitment, which in turn drives further fire. The research was conducted by a team working with the Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation, an organisation representing traditional owners. The team reconstructed 1,000 years of vegetation and fire history at Purghagoolah, a lake in Croajingolong National Park in Gippsland, Victoria, by analysing pollen and charcoal particles in a metre-long sediment core. Fletcher noted that prior to colonisation, the area was a “cared for and managed landscape.” Cultural burning involves First Nations people using low-temperature fire to maintain landscapes through a “right time, right place” approach, which differs from government hazard reduction practices. While these practices are still used in parts of Australia as of October 7, 2026, Fletcher suggested the research provides scientific evidence for integrating Indigenous knowledge into modern fire management. Adam Morton, a fire scientist at the University of Tasmania who was not an author of the paper, described the research as significant to the understanding of landscape change resulting from the loss of Indigenous fire management.

cards.headline: Two scientists awarded 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discoveries regarding mirror-image molecules

The scientists received the prize for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, which demonstrated how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror-image forms of a molecule. The two recipients will each receive an equal share of a 12 million Swedish kronor prize, valued at approximately £900,000. This property, known as chirality, allows molecules to exist in two forms that contain the same atoms but act as mirror images of one another. Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London, noted that because many molecules in the body are chiral, the different versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways, potentially leading to weakened or different drug effects. The Heads of State meeting for the AU Mid-Year Coordination Summit is set to take place on September 27, 2026. These gatherings aim to bring together governments, businesses, and financial institutions to explore investment opportunities and strengthen partnerships to advance Africa’s economic integration and sustainable development.

During the proceedings, President Mahama is scheduled to deliver a keynote address at a plenary session titled “Investing in Health: Manufacturing and Regional Value Chains.” His address is expected to examine healthcare as a social responsibility and a strategic economic sector with investment potential, with a focus on manufacturing and the development of regional value chains. Additionally, President Mahama is expected to hold bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the events, including talks with President el-Sisi.

cards.headline: Megapoll finds nearly half of UK voters support rejoining EU

pages.text: A poll by the Messina Group (TMG) found that almost half of all voters support Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s preference to rejoin the European Union after the next election. The findings suggest that renegotiating the UK’s relationship with the EU could increase the Labour Party's vote share by as much as seven points, provided the prime minister offers a fresh referendum and campaigns for re-entry into the bloc. Regarding the decision-making process, almost a third of voters stated an in-out referendum would be required first, while more than one in six believed a general election mandate would be sufficient, and an equal proportion felt parliament could make the decision. On September 29, 2026, Burnham used his first Labour conference speech as leader to announce a review of options for Britain’s future relationship with Europe, noting that these options should include rejoining entirely.

The poll results come amid internal political caution within the Labour government. Two-thirds of cabinet ministers, including Burnham, first secretary Louise Haigh, chancellor John Healey, and foreign secretary Ed Miliband, represent seats that backed Brexit and have previously stated they would respect the 2016 vote. Some Labour MPs have expressed concerns that testing public support for rejoining could pose political risks and potentially benefit Reform. Several ministers have also publicly cautioned against the move: deputy leader Lucy Powell stated going beyond inherited EU reset plans was “not possible nor desirable”; trade secretary Jonathan Reynolds cited “constitutional questions” causing business uncertainty; and home secretary Shabana Mahmood noted that rejoining is “not a simple, straightforward thing” and that costs might be unacceptable.

cards.headline: Kofi Bentil describes arrest of Manhyia South MP as political witch-hunt

pages.text: Kofi Bentil, a lawyer and Senior Vice-President of IMANI Ghana, has characterized the arrest of Manhyia South MP Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah by the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO) as a politically motivated witch-hunt. Speaking during a JoyNews Newsfile discussion on Saturday, October 3, Bentil, who is also a business strategy lecturer and consultant, alleged that members of both the New Patriotic Party (NPP) and the National Democratic Congress (NDC) recognize the arrest as a political attack. Bentil questioned the specific charges against the legislator, noting reports that he was deemed to have taken more than proper fees from both sides.

The arrest followed a disputed attempt to take the MP into custody at the Accra High Court on September 23. EOCO stated the action was intended to secure the MP's attendance after previous invitations were not honored. However, Baffour Awuah’s lawyers challenged this account, asserting that a representative of his law firm had already engaged with investigators and provided the requested information. During the same broadcast, legal practitioner and NDC Communications Team member Theophelious Dzimegah Jnr defended EOCO, arguing the agency was performing its legally mandated duties without violating the MP's human rights and maintained that Baffour Awuah should have submitted to investigators due to his connection to the law firm involved in the transactions under investigation.

cards.headline: EOCO working with Attorney-General to arraign Manhyia South MP before weekend court

pages.text: The Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO) stated on October 2, 2026, that it is working with the Office of the Attorney-General to bring Manhyia South MP Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah before a weekend court. According to a statement issued by EOCO, the move follows the MP's voluntary surrender to the agency at 10 a.m. on October 1, 2026. EOCO noted that the action aligns with constitutional timeframes and procedural requirements governing bail. The agency also dismissed reports claiming the MP had been granted GH¢50 million bail, urging the public to disregard such information. Investigations and other procedural processes involving the MP remain ongoing.

On October 2, 2026, Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin questioned EOCO's decision to search the MP's residence. Speaking to the media after visiting Mr. Awuah in EOCO custody, Mr. Afenyo-Markin claimed the MP found the decision puzzling because he believed the court order obtained by the agency specifically authorized a search of his law firm in Dzorwulu rather than his residence. Mr. Afenyo-Markin stated that the issue arose after EOCO informed the detained MP of their intention to search his residence and noted that the court had directed the order be served on Speaker of Parliament Alban Bagbin.

cards.headline: Magnitude 4.8 earthquake strikes near Leongatha, Victoria

pages.text: Geoscience Australia detected a preliminary magnitude 4.8 earthquake at 2:01 a.m. near Leongatha, located 130km south-east of Melbourne. The quake was estimated to have occurred at a depth of approximately 10km. Tremors were felt across Melbourne's eastern suburbs and other areas including Narre Warren, Garfield, Preston, Heidelberg Heights, and Venus Bay. Geoscience Australia reported receiving thousands of accounts from individuals who felt the earthquake. The Bureau of Meteorology stated there was no tsunami threat resulting from the event. The earthquake occurred in South Gippsland, a region identified as being among the most active seismic zones in Australia. This event was the largest recorded in the state since a magnitude 5.0 earthquake on the Great Ocean Road in 2023. An aftershock with a magnitude of 3.1 was recorded 55 minutes after the initial quake. Additionally, a magnitude 3.3 earthquake was recorded on the morning of October 1, 2026, at Yarram, approximately 80km east of Leongatha.

cards.headline: Government intervention begins at Mallam Junction to address recurring flooding

pages.text: Renewed government intervention at Mallam Junction in Ghana is underway to address landfill, drainage, and environmental challenges linked to recurring flooding in the area. According to MyJoyOnline, the efforts aim to provide a lasting solution for local residents, motorists, and businesses. The initiative follows engagements initiated from Jubilee House under Chief of Staff Julius Debrah, which involved the Weija-Gbawe Municipal Assembly, relevant government agencies, and private-sector stakeholders to focus on blocked drainage channels and landfill issues surrounding the junction. This activity is part of broader government efforts to restore waterways and drainage systems in flood-prone areas across Greater Accra. The Post-Flood Mitigation Task Force is coordinating the exercise with the stated objective of restoring waterway integrity and reducing flooding impacts in affected communities.

In August, work commenced to reclaim the Lafa water retention basin at Mallam. The 48 Engineer Regiment of the Ghana Armed Forces was deployed to remove years of accumulated silt and solid waste that had reduced the basin's capacity to retain stormwater. The operation also included the removal of illegal structures and includes plans to construct protective embankments. Local residents and businesses have expressed hope that the sustained government presence at drainage and landfill sites represents a departure from previous interventions that typically intensified only after heavy rainfall. The involvement of the Weija-Gbawe Municipal Assembly is noted as critical for local sanitation enforcement, drainage maintenance, and monitoring activities around the affected areas.
